line: Picture a small American town in the year {1932|nineteen thirty two}. A man in a neat hat walks
down Main Street to the bank where he has saved for twenty years.
And the doors are locked. A paper sign hangs in the window. The bank is closed.
For good.
Now picture that same scene in thousands of towns, all
across the country.
One out of every four grown-ups,
with no job.
Families living in little towns made of cardboard and tin.
Farmers pouring milk onto the road
because nobody could
afford to buy it.
This really happened.
Less than a hundred years ago.
It was called the Great Depression,
and it was the biggest economic
slump of the modern world.
And here's the craziest part.
It didn't start with people being sad.
It started with people being way, way too happy.
Today, I'm going to explain the entire Great Depression
like you're five years old.
No boring charts.
No confusing money words.
Just a story.
And by the end,
you'll understand something most adults don't.
Why it happened.
Why it lasted for ten long years.
And why people still
talk about it today.
Let's go.
Chapter one. The biggest party in history.
To understand the crash,
you have to understand the party.
It's the {1920s|nineteen twenties}.
The First World War just ended,
and America came out of it rich.
Factories are booming.
And suddenly, there's all this amazing new stuff.
Cars.
Radios.
Refrigerators.
Washing machines.
Things that felt like magic.
People called it the Roaring Twenties.
Jazz music.
Dancing all night.
Everyone felt like the good times would never end.
But there was a catch.
A lot of families couldn't actually
afford all this new stuff.
So stores came up with a clever idea.
Buy now. Pay later.
Think of it like this.
Imagine a candy shop that tells every kid,
take all the candy you like today, and
just pay a little bit every week.
Sounds amazing, right?
So every kid in town fills up their pockets.
Everyone looks rich.
Everyone has new stuff.
But underneath, a lot of families owe
more than they can really handle.
Remember that. It matters.
Chapter two. The magic money machine.
Now, there was one place
where people were getting rich
faster than anywhere else.
The stock market.
So what is the stock market?
Let's say a kid named Sam has a lemonade stand.
Sam wants to grow,
so Sam splits the lemonade stand
into one hundred tiny pieces
and sells them.
Each piece is called a share.
If someone buys one,
they own a tiny piece of Sam's lemonade stand.
If the stand does great,
everyone wants a piece,
and the price of each piece goes up.
If the stand does badly,
nobody wants it,
and the price goes down.
That's it. That's the stock market.
Just millions of people buying and
selling tiny pieces of companies.
In the {1920s|nineteen twenties}, prices only went one direction.
Up. Up. Up.
People were doubling their money.
Regular people, like waiters and shop workers,
started buying shares because their neighbors seemed to be getting rich.
And here's where it gets risky.
Many of them
used something called buying on margin.
It works like this.
Imagine a kid wants a lemonade
share that costs ten dollars,
but only has one dollar.
So the kid borrows the other nine from a grown-up.
If the price goes up, great,
the loan gets paid back and the kid keeps the extra.
But if the price goes down,
the kid still owes the grown-up nine dollars,
even if the share is now worth almost nothing.
People were making huge bets with borrowed money,
on prices they assumed would rise forever.
There's a famous story about this.
A wealthy businessman was getting his shoes shined,
and the shoeshine boy started giving him tips
about which shares to buy.
The businessman thought,
if even the shoeshine boy is in the market,
everyone is in.
There's no one left to buy.
And he quietly sold everything.
Whether that story is completely true or not,
the lesson was right.
The party was about to end.
Chapter three. The crash.
October {1929|nineteen twenty nine}.
Prices start wobbling.
Then dropping.
On Thursday, October twenty-fourth, worry spreads fast, and
people start selling all at once.
History calls it Black Thursday.
The big banks stepped in and
bought shares to calm everyone down.
And it worked...
for a few days.
Then came Tuesday, October twenty-ninth.
Black Tuesday. One of
the worst days the stock market had ever seen.
Everyone wanted to sell.
Almost nobody wanted to buy.
And remember all those people who
borrowed money to buy shares?
Now the lenders wanted
their money
back.
To pay them, people had to sell even more shares.
Which pushed prices down even more.
Which made even more people sell.
It's like a line of dominoes.
One falls, then the next, then the next,
faster and faster.
And it didn't stop in {1929|nineteen twenty nine}.
The market kept sliding for almost three years.
By the summer of {1932|nineteen thirty two},
the stock market had lost about
ninety percent of its value.
Imagine a hundred-dollar toy collection
turning into ten dollars.
But wait.
Here's the twist most people get wrong.
The stock market crash was NOT the Great Depression.
Most Americans didn't even own shares.
The crash was just the first domino.
What came next was much bigger.
Chapter four. When the
banks closed their doors.
Okay. Let's talk about banks.
Because this is where the real trouble happened.
A lot of people imagine a bank
like a giant piggy bank.
Money goes in,
and it just sits there in a
vault.
But that's not how it works.
A bank lends most of
that money out to other people.
To buy houses.
To start businesses.
It only keeps a
little bit in the vault,
because on a normal day, only a few people
come to take some out.
Now imagine a small town.
One day, a rumor goes
around that the bank might be in trouble.
A few people go to take their savings out.
Their neighbors notice, and they go too.
Then their friends.
Soon the whole town is standing
in a long line outside the bank.
But the money isn't all there.
Most of it has been lent out.
The bank runs out of cash,
and it closes its doors. Historians call
this a bank run.
And back then,
there was no insurance
for bank savings. If a bank closed,
families often lost a big part of what they had saved. Then the
next town hears the news.
They worry
too. They line up at their own bank.
And that bank closes as well.
Worry spread from town to town.
Across the {1930s|nineteen thirties}, about nine thousand American banks failed.
Millions of families lost money they had worked years to save.
Chapter five. The doom loop.
Now here's where it turns from a bad year
into a ten-year slump.
Imagine a toy factory.
Families have less money,
so they stop buying toys.
The factory isn't selling anything,
so it lets half its workers go.
Now those workers have no paycheck.
So they stop buying shoes, and food, and clothes.
So the shoe store lets its workers go.
And the clothing store.
And the restaurant.
Every family that stops spending means
someone else loses their job.
And every person who loses their job stops spending.
It's a loop.
A doom loop.
And it keeps spinning.
On top of that, prices started falling.
And you might think, wait,
cheaper stuff is good, right?
Not here.
If a farmer's corn sells for half the price,
but the farmer still owes the
same amount on the farm,
that debt suddenly feels twice as heavy. Many
farmers couldn't keep up, and
they lost their farms.
By {1933|nineteen thirty three}, about one in four
American workers had no job at all.
One in four.
Think of four people you know.
Now imagine one of them out of work, for years.
And many of the ones who still had jobs
saw their hours and pay cut.
Chapter six. The mistakes that made it worse.
Now you might be asking.
Why didn't anyone fix it?
Well. The people in charge made some big mistakes.
Three of them, actually.
Mistake number one. The money shrank.
America has something called the Federal Reserve.
Think of it as the boss of money.
Its job is to make sure
there's enough money flowing around.
But when banks were collapsing,
it mostly stood back and let it happen.
The amount of money in the
country shrank by about a third.
Imagine playing a board game
where someone keeps taking money out of the box.
Pretty soon, nobody can play.
Mistake number two. The gold rule.
Back then, many countries followed
something called the gold standard.
It meant every dollar had to be backed
by real gold sitting in a vault.
Sounds safe, right?
But it meant governments couldn't create more money
when people desperately needed it.
Their hands were tied.
And here's a fun fact.
The countries that broke this rule first,
like Britain in {1931|nineteen thirty one},
generally started recovering sooner.
Mistake number three. The playground fight.
In {1930|nineteen thirty}, America passed a
law called the Smoot-Hawley Tariff.
It put big taxes on
things bought from other countries.
The idea was to protect American jobs.
But imagine you're on the playground,
and you tell everyone,
"I'm not trading my snacks with you anymore."
What do the other kids do?
They stop trading with you too.
That's exactly what happened.
Other countries struck back with their own taxes.
World trade collapsed by about two-thirds.
Factories everywhere lost their customers.
And the president at the time, Herbert Hoover,
did try a few things.
But he mostly believed the economy
would heal on its own,
and that the government shouldn't step in too much.
People were waiting for help.
And it wasn't coming.
Chapter seven. What life actually felt like.
Let's step away from the
money stuff for a second.
Because behind every number, there was a real family.
People lost their homes
and built little shacks out of wood scraps,
cardboard, and metal.
Whole towns of them.
People angrily called them Hoovervilles, after the president.
Long lines of men in suits and hats
stood for hours,
just to get a free bowl
of soup and a piece of bread.
Young people jumped onto moving freight trains,
riding across the country,
looking for any kind of work.
Kids wore clothes made out of flour sacks.
Families ate whatever they could find.
And then, as if things couldn't get worse,
nature joined in.
In the middle of America, farmers had plowed up
so much grassland
that when a terrible drought hit,
the soil just dried up and blew away.
Giant clouds of dust, taller than buildings,
rolled across the sky and turned day into night.
It was called the Dust Bowl.
Thousands of families packed everything into old cars
and drove west, hoping for a new start.
And it wasn't just America.
The Depression spread across the whole world.
In Germany, where people were already struggling,
millions lost their jobs.
Angry and desperate, many turned to a man
who promised to make everything better.
His name was Adolf Hitler.
And in {1933|nineteen thirty three}, he came to power.
The Great Depression didn't just break the economy.
It helped set the stage
for the Second World War.
Chapter eight. The man who said "don't be afraid."
In {1933|nineteen thirty three}, America got a new president.
Franklin D. Roosevelt.
People called him FDR.
And on his very first day,
he said one of the
most famous lines in history.
"The only thing we have to fear
is fear itself."
Think about why that's so smart.
Remember the bank runs?
Banks didn't fail only because they were bad.
They failed because people were scared.
And fear made people run,
and running made the banks fail,
which made people even more scared.
So FDR did something bold.
He closed every bank in the
country for a few days.
A bank holiday.
Inspectors checked them,
and only the healthy ones were allowed to reopen.
Then he did something no
president had really done before.
He got on the radio
and talked to Americans like a friend
sitting by the fireplace.
He explained, in simple words, how banks worked,
and why it was safe
to put their money back.
These talks were called fireside chats.
And here's the amazing part.
When the banks reopened,
people actually lined up...
to put their money back in.
Fear started to turn into hope.
Chapter nine. The New Deal.
FDR didn't stop there.
He launched a huge set of
programs called the New Deal.
Let's keep it simple.
First, protect people's money.
The government created deposit insurance, the FDIC.
It means if your bank fails,
the government pays you back.
That's why today, bank runs like the {1930s|nineteen thirties}
are so much rarer.
Second, give people jobs.
The government hired millions of people
to build roads, bridges, schools,
parks, and dams.
Young men planted billions of trees.
Artists painted murals.
Writers wrote guidebooks.
Some people called it wasteful.
But it put paychecks back into people's pockets.
And remember the doom loop?
Paychecks mean spending.
Spending means more jobs.
The loop started spinning the other way.
Third, a safety net.
Social Security was created,
so older people and people who couldn't work
would have some money to live on.
Fourth, rules for the stock market.
A new watchdog, the SEC,
was created to stop the
kind of wild, reckless betting
that started this whole mess.
America also loosened its ties to the gold rule,
which let more money flow.
And it worked.
Slowly.
The economy started growing again.
But then... another mistake.
In {1937|nineteen thirty seven}, leaders thought the danger was over.
The government cut spending,
and the Federal Reserve tightened money again.
And boom.
The economy fell right back into a slump.
It was like taking off a cast
before the bone had healed.
Chapter ten. How it finally ended.
So what finally ended the Great Depression?
Sadly, it was a war.
When the Second World War began,
America started building planes, tanks,
ships, and weapons at an enormous scale.
Factories ran day and night.
Millions of people joined the military,
and millions more went to work in factories,
including many women for the first time.
Suddenly, there were more jobs than workers.
The doom loop was finally broken.
And here's a number that will blow your mind.
If you had bought stocks at
the very top in {1929|nineteen twenty nine},
you would have had to wait until {1954|nineteen fifty four}
to get back to even.
Twenty-five years.
Chapter eleven. Why this still matters to you.
Okay. So why should you care
about something that happened almost a hundred years ago?
Because the world learned from it.
In {2008|two thousand eight}, when banks started collapsing again,
leaders remembered the {1930s|nineteen thirties}.
The Federal Reserve pumped money into the system
instead of letting it shrink.
Governments stepped in fast.
And in {2020|twenty twenty}, when the world shut down,
the same lessons kicked in again.
Those weren't perfect solutions.
But they were a lot better
than standing back and waiting.
And if you have money in a bank today,
it's protected, partly because of the Great Depression.
So let's recap, like you're five.
People bought too much stuff they couldn't pay for.
They bet borrowed money on stocks.
Prices crashed.
Scared people pulled their money out of banks.
Banks collapsed.
People stopped spending.
Businesses closed.
Leaders made it worse.
Life got really, really hard.
Until a president told everyone not to be afraid,
the government stepped in,
and finally, a world war changed everything.
But the biggest lesson isn't about money at all.
The Great Depression shows us that fear is contagious.
When everyone panics at once,
even strong things can break.
And hope is contagious too.
If you learned something today,
share this with someone who's always wondered
how the Great Depression actually happened.
And subscribe,
because next time, I'm explaining another piece of history
that changed the world...
like you're five.
See you there.
